questions.question: What is the best definition of a *mutagen*?
questions.answer: A mutagen is an agent (for example UV radiation, X-rays or certain chemicals) that causes mutation, that is, genetic change (B). A is the definition of a mutation.
options: A change in the structure of DNA.
An agent that causes genetic change.
The action or process of nucleotide change.
The rearrangement of sections of chromosomes and genes.

questions.question: Which of the following cell types initiates the secondary immune response depicted below?
questions.answer: On second exposure to the same antigen, memory B cells formed during the primary response recognise it and rapidly divide into plasma cells, giving a faster, larger antibody response (B).
options: cytotoxic T cell
memory B cell
helper T cell
suppressor T cell

questions.question:
Four ways of being immune are:

1. having memory cells after an infection
2. having memory cells after being injected with dead bacteria
3. being injected with antibodies
4. receiving antibodies from breast milk

Which row in the table correctly shows the types of immunity?

| | natural active | artificial active | natural passive | artificial passive |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| B | 1 | 2 | 4 | 3 |
| C | 2 | 1 | 3 | 4 |
| D | 2 | 1 | 4 | 3 |
questions.answer: Active immunity means the body makes its own memory cells: after an infection it is natural (1), after a vaccine (dead bacteria) it is artificial (2). Passive immunity means antibodies are received: from breast milk it is natural (4), by injection it is artificial (3). So the row is 1, 2, 4, 3 (B).
options: A
B
C
D

questions.question: A pathogen was found to be prokaryotic, contain DNA and have a cell wall. How would it be classified?
questions.answer: Prokaryotic cells with DNA and a cell wall are bacteria. Viruses are not cellular, and fungi and protozoa are eukaryotic (D).
options: Virus
Fungus
Protozoan
Bacterium

questions.question: Skin grafting involves the transplantation of healthy skin which can be used to cover damaged skin, for example due to burns. A graft of skin tissue received from a different person is usually rejected by the recipient's body. Which statement about graft rejection is correct?
questions.answer: The paper's key is D: the recipient's immune system recognises the donor cells' surface antigens as foreign, and B-lymphocytes produce antibodies that react with them. (Note: T-cell-mediated rejection, as in B, is also a recognised mechanism; C is wrong because T-lymphocytes do not make antibodies.)
options: The graft is rejected by B-lymphocytes because T-lymphocytes are not stimulated to produce antibodies.
The graft is rejected by T-lymphocytes because they circulate in the blood and can gather at the graft site.
The graft is rejected by T-lymphocytes because the graft tissue causes T-lymphocytes to release antibodies.
The graft is rejected by B-lymphocytes because they make and release antibodies which react with the surface antigens on the graft cells.

questions.question:
The diagram below shows one way of testing the effect of an antibiotic on bacteria. The table shows the results of testing five different types of bacteria using the method above. Zones of less than 13 mm show the presence of resistant bacteria.

| Type of bacteria | Diameter of zone with no bacterial growth after 5 days (mm) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 14.30 |
| 2 | 0.00 |
| 3 | 10.90 |
| 4 | 0.00 |
| 5 | 20.40 |

Which statement can be supported by this data?
questions.answer: Zones under 13 mm indicate resistance. Types 2 (0.00 mm), 3 (10.90 mm) and 4 (0.00 mm) are below 13 mm, so only these are resistant (D). Type 3 is not treatable, so A is wrong; the data cannot show what happens over time (B, C).
options: The antibiotic can be used to treat bacteria types 1 and 3 only.
All the types of bacteria become resistant to antibiotics over time.
Type 5 of the bacteria can never become resistant to the antibiotic.
Only types 2, 3 and 4 of the bacteria show resistance to the antibiotic.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a function of a macrophage?
questions.answer: Macrophages are phagocytes found in tissues; they engulf pathogens and secrete cytokines that signal other immune cells (B). Histamine is released by mast cells and basophils, antigens are not produced by macrophages, and cytotoxins are released by cytotoxic T cells and NK cells.
options: They release histamines.
They are found in tissues and secrete cytokines in response to infection.
They circulate in the blood and produce antigens in response to infection.
They can leave the blood and secrete cytotoxins when exposed to damaged cells.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the benefit(s) of artificial insemination of dairy cattle?
questions.answer: Semen from one high-quality bull can be collected, diluted and used to inseminate many cows on many farms, spreading desirable milk-production traits (C). The offspring are not clones (A) or genetically modified (D).
options: The process creates genetically identical offspring that all produce good milk yield.
It decreases genetic diversity by introducing the same genes to different populations on different farms.
It enables a large number of cows to be inseminated with sperm from a bull with desirable milk production traits.
The process creates genetically modified calves that may produce milk in the future that is safe for human consumption.

questions.question:
Which row is the best comparison of the daughter cell produced in each process?

| | Mitosis | Meiosis |
|---|---|---|
| A | Identical to parent; identical to each other; homologous pairs of chromosomes | Different to parent; different to each other; unpaired chromosomes |
| B | Different to parent; identical to each other; homologous pairs of chromosomes | Identical to parent; different to each other; unpaired chromosomes |
| C | Identical to parent; different to each other; unpaired chromosomes | Different to parent; identical to each other; homologous pairs of chromosomes |
| D | Identical to parent; identical to each other; unpaired chromosomes | Different to parent; different to each other; homologous pairs of chromosomes |
questions.answer: Mitosis produces diploid daughter cells genetically identical to the parent cell and to each other, with homologous pairs. Meiosis produces haploid gametes that differ from the parent and from each other (crossing over, independent assortment) and have unpaired chromosomes (A).
options: A
B
C
D

questions.question: Which statement best describes how cloning might be used to assist human health?
questions.answer: Therapeutic cloning could produce tissues and organs genetically matched to a patient to replace diseased or damaged ones (C). A clone is a separate organism, so A is wrong.
options: Human clones will mean an individual can 'live' forever.
Antibiotic resistant bacteria can be used to produce medicines.
Human organs could be cloned to replace diseased or damaged organs.
Food from cloned plants and animals can be modified to be healthier for human consumption.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a physiological adaptation in an endotherm that assists in maintaining homeostasis?
questions.answer: Physiological adaptations are internal functions. Vasoconstriction of surface blood vessels reduces heat loss in a cold environment (C). A is structural and B and D are behavioural (D is also an ectotherm).
options: Animals in cold climates having thick fur coats.
A dog moving into the shade to keep cool on a hot day.
Surface blood vessels in a human constricting on a cold day.
Lizards moving into the sunlight to raise their body temperature.

questions.question: The diagram models the process of fertilisation (sperm cells surrounding an egg cell). Which of the following is an appropriate evaluation of this model?
questions.answer: An evaluation of a model judges its strengths and limitations. D identifies a strength (simplicity) and a limitation (inaccurate relative sizes). A is only a description, B is only negative, and C wrongly claims reliability (a single sperm enters the egg, so not all stages are shown) (D).
options: The diagram shows the entry of sperm cells into the egg.
The diagram has some downfalls, such as the egg is too large.
The diagram is a very reliable model of fertilisation because it shows all the stages of fertilisation.
The diagram is good because it depicts fertilisation in a simple way, despite inaccuracies such as the size of cells.

questions.question: Grapefruit originated from a cross between an orange and a pomelo. What is this an example of?
questions.answer: Crossing two varieties/species to combine desirable traits is selective breeding (C). Transgenics involves inserting genes from another species.
options: Cloning
Transgenics
Selective breeding
Artificial insemination

questions.question: A chemical mutagen is known to cause significant damage to DNA structure through the disruption of the normal base-pairing process. A graph shows a positive linear relationship between mutagen vapour concentration (ppm) on the horizontal axis and the number of base-pairing errors on the vertical axis. Which of the following statements correctly describes the trend observed?
questions.answer: The independent variable (mutagen vapour concentration) is on the horizontal axis and the dependent variable (base-pairing errors) increases with it, so more mutagen leads to more errors (C).
options: An increased frequency of base-pairing errors leads to increased mutations.
An increased number of base-pairing errors leads to increased vapour production.
An increase in mutagen vapour concentration leads to an increase in the frequency of base-pairing errors.
An increase in mutagen vapour concentration leads to a decrease in the frequency of base-pairing errors.

questions.question: Some organisms have genotypes that produce three different phenotypes, for example a red flower crossed with a white flower to produce a pink flower. If two of these pink flowers were crossed, which of the following graphs would correctly represent the offspring of this cross?
questions.answer: This is incomplete dominance: pink flowers are heterozygous (RW). RW × RW gives 1 RR (red) : 2 RW (pink) : 1 WW (white), i.e. 25% : 50% : 25%, which is graph C (three bars with the middle one twice as tall).
options: Graph A
Graph B
Graph C
Graph D

questions.question: The graph shows the changes of three hormones during gestation (pregnancy). Which of the statements below best identifies the changes in hormone levels shown over the gestation period?
questions.answer: The curve peaking at about 8 weeks and then falling is hCG. The two other curves (oestrogen and progesterone) rise steadily through gestation and fall sharply at birth (about 40 weeks) (C).
options: hCG and oestrogen both rise and stay high in concentration from 24 weeks onwards.
Progesterone levels peak at 8 weeks then drop when the placenta is formed.
Both oestrogen and progesterone gradually rise in concentration until birth where they both rapidly decline at around 40 weeks.
hCG, produced by cells surrounding the embryo and then the placenta, peaks at around week 36 and can be detected in urine tests.

questions.question: Analyse the diagram which shows two pairs of homologous chromosomes and their allele arrangement. Assuming there is no crossing over, which of the following shows all the possible genotypes for the gametes formed in this organism?
questions.answer: Without crossing over, alleles on the same chromosome stay together. Pair 1 chromosomes are A B c and A b C; pair 2 chromosomes are D e and d E. Independent assortment gives 2 × 2 = 4 gametes: ABc+De, ABc+dE, AbC+De, AbC+dE, i.e. ABcDe, ABcdE, AbCDe, AbCdE (A).
options: ABcDe, ABcdE, AbCDe, AbCdE
AbCdE, ABCdE, AbCDE, AbCdE
ABcDE, ABcdE, AbCDe, AbDdE
AbcDE, ABcdE, AbCDe, ABcdE

questions.question: Which of the following represents the DNA sequence that codes for the mRNA strand shown below? mRNA: 5'–CUAACG–3'
questions.answer: The DNA template strand is complementary to the mRNA and antiparallel: mRNA 5'-C U A A C G-3' pairs with 3'-G A T T G C-5'. DNA contains thymine, not uracil, so B and C are wrong (A).
options: 3'–GATTGC–5'
3'–GAUUGC–5'
3'–CGUUAG–5'
3'–CGTTAG–5'

questions.question: Analyse the graph which shows blood glucose regulation (the effects of insulin and glucagon on blood sugar levels). Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.answer: H is where blood glucose has fallen below its set point, so glucagon is released to raise it; this is where glucagon is highest (B). Insulin peaks when blood glucose is highest, not at A, and the set point is about 90 mg/100 mL, not 140.
options: Insulin is highest at A.
Glucagon is highest at H.
Insulin levels are high whenever the blood glucose levels reach 90 mg/mL.
According to this graph the optimal blood glucose concentration is 140 mg/100 mL.

questions.question: There were 15 cases of thyroid cancer recorded in Iceland between December 2009 and January 2011. The graph shows, for each case, the month of diagnosis (▲) and month of recovery (▼) or death (X) from the disease. Iceland has a population of 330 000 people. Which of the options below was the incidence rate (per 100 000) of thyroid cancer from March to October 2010?
questions.answer: Incidence counts new cases (diagnoses ▲) in the period: six cases were diagnosed between March and October 2010. Incidence rate $=\dfrac{6}{330\,000}\times100\,000\approx1.8$ per 100 000 (B).

questions.question: The diagram shows a stage of polypeptide synthesis. Identify the stage of polypeptide synthesis in this diagram.
questions.answer: Translation.

questions.question: The diagram shows translation at a ribosome, in which tRNA molecules with anti-codons bring amino acids to the mRNA. Why is the anti-codon significant in this process?
questions.answer: The anti-codon is a triplet of bases on a tRNA molecule that is complementary to a codon on the mRNA. This means that the tRNA, with its attached amino acid, binds to the correct codon, so amino acids are joined in the correct order to form a functional polypeptide (protein).

questions.question: The diagram shows the process of cross-pollination in plants, similar to the method Mendel used in his experiments (pollen transferred with a brush from one flower to the stigma of another flower whose anthers have been removed). Which step ensures the validity of the cross-pollination? Justify your answer.
questions.answer: Removal of the anthers. This prevents self-pollination, ensuring that only the transferred pollen fertilises the ova, so the parents of the offspring are known and the results of the cross are valid.

questions.question: The pea plant species in the diagram has two phenotypes for pea colour, green and yellow. Both parent plants are homozygous, and the plant providing the pollen produces yellow peas. Only green peas were produced (see diagram). Identify the dominant and recessive phenotypes for pea colour in this species.
questions.answer: Dominant: green. Recessive: yellow. (Crossing two homozygous parents gave only green offspring, so green is dominant.)

questions.question: In the cross-pollination in the diagram, both parent plants are homozygous and only green peas were produced. Determine the phenotype and genotype ratios of the offspring produced when crossing two plants grown from the peas in this diagram.
questions.answer:
Let G = green (dominant) and g = yellow (recessive). The parents of the diagram were GG and gg, so the peas produced (and the plants grown from them) are all heterozygous, Gg. Cross Gg × Gg:

| | G | g |
|---|---|---|
| **G** | GG | Gg |
| **g** | Gg | gg |

Genotype ratio: 1 GG : 2 Gg : 1 gg. Phenotype ratio: 3 green : 1 yellow. (Note that the genotype ratio is different from the phenotype ratio, because GG and Gg are both green.)

questions.question: The diagram shows the gene pool of a population over 20 generations (R and r alleles). Describe how the population has changed over the 20 generations.
questions.answer: In generation 1 both alleles are common and the population contains RR, Rr and rr individuals (the R and r alleles are about equally frequent). By generation 10 the R allele has become much less frequent, and by generation 20 the R allele has disappeared from the gene pool, leaving only the r allele (all individuals are rr).

questions.question: The diagram shows the gene pool of a population over 20 generations, in which the R allele declines and is lost. Explain how the changes in the gene pool may have occurred.
questions.answer: Natural selection may have acted on the population. If the R allele produces a trait that is not favourable in this environment, individuals with that trait are less likely to survive and reproduce, so they pass on fewer R alleles. Individuals with the rr genotype are better suited, survive and pass on r alleles. Over 20 generations the frequency of R decreased until it was removed from the gene pool. (Genetic drift in a small population could also cause an allele to be lost by chance.)

questions.question: The diagram shows the gene pool of a population in generation 10, which contains 32 alleles (8 are R and 24 are r). Calculate the allele frequency for the two alleles present in generation 10.
questions.answer: Frequency of R $=\dfrac{8}{32}=0.25$ (25%). Frequency of r $=\dfrac{24}{32}=0.75$ (75%), which is also $1-0.25$.

questions.question: Analyse the pedigree below showing a genetic condition expressed in a family. Determine the pattern of inheritance shown in this pedigree and identify the genotypes of individuals 1 and 16. Use the letter 'A' or 'a' to represent alleles.
questions.answer: Pattern of inheritance: autosomal recessive. Individuals 8 and 9 are both unaffected but have an affected child (17), so the condition is recessive, and an affected daughter (17) of an unaffected father (9) shows it is not X-linked. Individual 1 is affected: genotype aa. Individual 16 is unaffected, and both parents (8 and 9) must be carriers (Aa), so 16 is either AA or Aa.

questions.question: Analyse the pedigree. The condition is autosomal recessive, and individual 16 is unaffected with a genotype of AA or Aa. If individual 16 has a child with an affected partner (who has the genetic condition), what are the chances this child will be affected? Show any relevant working.
questions.answer:
The affected partner is aa. If 16 is Aa: Aa × aa gives Aa, aa, Aa, aa, so 2 in 4 (50%) of the children would be affected. If 16 is AA: AA × aa gives all Aa, so 0% would be affected.

| | A | a |
|---|---|---|
| **a** | Aa | aa |
| **a** | Aa | aa |

| | A | A |
|---|---|---|
| **a** | Aa | Aa |
| **a** | Aa | Aa |

Since 16's parents are both Aa, 16 is AA with probability 1/3 and Aa with probability 2/3, so the overall chance of an affected child is $\frac23\times\frac12=\frac13$ (about 33%). (Note: the school's example states '2 in 8 (25%)' for the Aa × aa cross, which is incorrect; the correct chance for that cross is 2 in 4, or 50%.)

questions.question: The diagram shows the result of crossing over during meiosis (a pair of replicated homologous chromosomes with alleles A/a, B/b and D/d). Identify the genotype of the parent cell.
questions.answer: Aa Bb Dd (the parent cell is heterozygous for all three genes).

questions.question: The diagram shows the neurons and parts of the body involved in a response to touching a hot object. Outline the stimulus–response pathway for this scenario by identifying the receptor, the effector and the response.
questions.answer: Stimulus: hot object. Receptor: thermoreceptors (pain/temperature receptors) in the skin. The sensory neuron carries the impulse to the CNS (spinal cord), where it is passed to a motor neuron. The motor neuron carries the impulse to the effector: the muscle cells in the arm. Response: the arm moves away from the hot object.

questions.question: DNA has both coding and non-coding segments, which vary in terms of biological function. The difference in function also means that the location of genetic mutations can change the impact on the function of the cell. Complete a table to distinguish between coding and non-coding DNA in terms of (i) biological function and (ii) an example of how biological function can be impacted by a mutation.
questions.answer:
| | Coding DNA | Non-coding DNA |
|---|---|---|
| Biological function | Codes for proteins (genes): transcribed to mRNA and translated into polypeptides, e.g. enzymes and structural proteins. | Does not code for proteins, but has other roles: regulation of gene expression (turning genes on and off), structural support for chromosomes (centromeres, telomeres), and coding for functional RNAs such as rRNA and tRNA. |
| Impact of a mutation | A point mutation (e.g. substitution causing a premature stop codon or a frameshift from an insertion or deletion) can change the amino acid sequence, producing a non-functional or altered protein and possibly disease. | A mutation in a regulatory region can turn genes on or off at the wrong time; a mutation in the centromere or telomere can cause chromosomes to be unable to separate correctly (non-disjunction) or to be damaged during replication, leading to aneuploidy or disease such as cancer. |

questions.question: Prostate cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in Australian men. Prostate Specific Antigen (PSA) is a protein secreted within the prostate gland. The normal function of this protein is as a component of semen. It is coded for by the *KLK3* gene on chromosome 19. PSA is normally very high in men who are developing prostate cancer. Using a flow diagram (or ordered steps), describe how the *KLK3* gene produces PSA.
questions.answer:
1. The KLK3 gene (in the nucleus) is transcribed: RNA polymerase makes KLK3 mRNA complementary to the DNA template.
2. The mRNA leaves the nucleus and moves into the cytoplasm, where it attaches to a ribosome.
3. Translation: tRNA molecules bring the corresponding amino acids to the codons on the mRNA.
4. The amino acids are joined into a polypeptide, which folds into the PSA protein.

questions.question: In a recent article it was stated that 11.8% of men who have metastatic (spreading) prostate cancer also have germ-line mutations in certain repair genes (Prichard et al, 2016). This is significantly more than in the general male population. What is meant by germ-line mutations?
questions.answer: A mutation occurring in a germ cell (cell that will become a gamete), which can then be inherited by offspring.

questions.question: Explain why the effect of germ-line mutations on organisms is more severe than somatic mutations.
questions.answer: A germ-line mutation is present in the gamete, so it can be passed on to offspring. The zygote carrying the mutation undergoes mitosis, producing every cell in the offspring's body with the mutation, and potentially many organisms in the population are affected. A somatic mutation, on the other hand, starts in one body cell, so only a patch of cells (within that organism) is affected and it is not inherited.

questions.question: Explain how mutations of genes which repair DNA might cause metastatic prostate cancer.
questions.answer: Errors in DNA repair genes can lead to failure to repair mistakes made during DNA replication. This allows mutations to accumulate in a cell in the prostate and results in uncontrollable cell proliferation, that is, cancer (which can then spread).

questions.question: Recent research has suggested that a diet high in processed meats correlates to a higher incidence of prostate cancer. Assess whether consuming processed meats has any scientific basis in causing prostate cancer.
questions.answer: Processed meats are high in carcinogens/mutagens, which are chemicals that can cause mutations in the DNA of cells exposed to them. A diet high in processed meats means these chemicals can accumulate in the prostate gland, increasing the chances of mutations occurring in prostate cells (including in genes that control the cell cycle and DNA repair), which can lead to cancer. Therefore there is a scientific basis for a causal link, although a correlation alone does not prove causation and other factors would also need to be considered.

questions.question: Genetic technologies such as DNA sequencing and DNA profiling can be used to determine inheritance patterns in a population. Compare the results obtained from these two technologies and discuss how they can be used to predict inheritance patterns and the spread of diseases.
questions.answer:
**DNA sequencing** determines the exact nucleotide sequence of a whole genome or of a specific DNA fragment/gene (using PCR and fluorescently labelled markers). The results show mutations, new alleles and diseased genes, and are used for medical diagnoses. It is more expensive but gives complete information. Examples: finding mutations in BRCA genes (tumour suppressor genes) to predict the likelihood of breast cancer and track mutations through a population; sequencing the genetic material of pathogens to track which serotypes/strains are spreading in a population (e.g. influenza, COVID-19) and designing vaccines for the most numerous strains in an outbreak.

**DNA profiling** uses restriction enzymes and PCR to compare short tandem repeats (STRs) at several loci (microsatellites) that vary between individuals, producing a unique banding pattern. It can collect data on a wide scale and track specific markers through populations and families, e.g. paternity testing and forensics. It is inexpensive. It shows which people are more predisposed to certain diseases (limited to risk factors), e.g. the link between sickle cell anaemia and resistance to malaria.

**Comparison:** sequencing reads the actual base sequence and identifies the cause of a disease (individual gene mutations), whereas profiling only compares patterns of markers and cannot show exactly which gene or mutation is present. Both can be used to predict inheritance patterns in populations: sequencing at a large scale and profiling for tracking markers or relatedness in a smaller scale. Used together they allow the spread of non-infectious genetic diseases and infectious disease to be predicted and monitored, helping targeted screening and public health responses.

questions.question: Cosmetics companies seek Kakadu Plum, or gubinge, found in north-western Australia, for its antioxidant- and nutrient-rich properties. For example, the cosmetics company Red Earth was using Kakadu Plum products to hand out on Qantas flights. The patenting of cloned animals, genetically modified crops and genetic materials such as the breast cancer gene is well publicised, but you can also patent natural products. Discuss the patenting of ingredients taken from Aboriginal Australian cultural and intellectual property.
questions.answer: Arguments against: patenting can fail to credit Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people or protect their rights, even though they have used and understood these plants for thousands of years (the knowledge was gained by Aboriginal people and the ingredients have been used for medicine, food and culture). Large companies may exploit this intellectual property for profit, and patents can limit the access of Aboriginal communities to plants that hold cultural significance and are part of their cultural property. Arguments for: ingredients like Kakadu Plum may have benefits for the wider population (e.g. the plant has medicinal properties), and companies already use these products, so patents and agreements (with Aboriginal protocols such as consent and benefit sharing) could provide economic benefits to Aboriginal communities. Overall, patenting is acceptable only if Aboriginal knowledge holders give consent, are acknowledged, and share the benefits.

questions.question: When a person is bitten by a venomous snake, the snake injects a toxin into the person. Antivenom is injected as treatment. This treatment is an example of passive immunity. Outline how the treatment with antivenom works and explain why it is essential to use passive immunity, rather than active immunity.
questions.answer: Antivenom is a solution of ready-made antibodies (from another animal) which are injected into the person; the antibodies bind to the venom (toxin) antigens and neutralise them. Passive immunity gives immediate protection. Active immunity would be too slow: it takes time for the body to stimulate B-plasma cells to produce the required antibodies (and form memory cells) and this delay might result in the death of the individual.

questions.question: A mixture of venoms from several snakes of the same species is used to make antivenom. Suggest why this makes a more effective antivenom.
questions.answer: Different snakes of the same species produce different venoms (different antigens, due to genetic diversity). A mixture means antibodies are made against all the different antigens, so the antivenom will be effective against the venom of any snake of that species, as it will bind to the different venoms.

questions.question: Antivenom is made by the vaccination of animals. Each animal is initially injected with a small volume of venom. Two weeks later, the animals are injected with a larger volume of venom following the purification of antibodies from the animal's blood plasma. Use your knowledge of the humoral immune response to explain this vaccination programme.
questions.answer: The first, small dose of venom is small enough not to harm the animal but its antigens stimulate the cloning of B-plasma cells, which produce specific antibodies, and B-memory cells are also produced. The larger second dose is given after about two weeks: memory B cells respond rapidly (the secondary response), producing a faster, larger concentration of antibodies. Because the animal has already built up immunity, the larger dose does not harm it. The antibodies are then purified from the animal's blood plasma and used as antivenom.

questions.question: Zika is a RNA virus, which can be spread by the *Aedes* mosquito. Most people infected with Zika experience no or very mild symptoms. An outbreak in South America was accompanied by an increase in the number of babies born with microcephaly. In 2016, concern was expressed by athletes travelling to the Olympics in Brazil. The advice given to anyone travelling to the Olympics was: use insect repellent and wear loose clothing that covers the body; keep windows closed at night and sleep under a mosquito net; avoid areas with poor sanitation and stagnant water. Identify the method of transmission of the Zika virus.
questions.answer: Vector (mosquito) transmission: the Zika virus is spread by the bite of the *Aedes* mosquito.

questions.question: The advice given to Olympic travellers to Brazil to reduce the risk of Zika infection was: use insect repellent and wear loose clothing that covers the body; keep windows closed at night and sleep under a mosquito net; avoid areas with poor sanitation and stagnant water. Outline how the preventative methods described would help reduce the chance of infection with Zika.
questions.answer: Each method prevents transmission of the virus: repellent and clothing covering the body and mosquito nets/closed windows prevent the mosquitoes from biting individuals and so stop the virus entering the person's body fluids; avoiding stagnant water and poor sanitation reduces contact with places where mosquitoes breed, reducing the number of vector mosquitoes (and so the chance of being bitten).

questions.question: The diagram shows how the Zika virus replicates inside a human cell (the virus binds to receptors, releases viral RNA, uses the host cell's replication and protein synthesis, assembles new viral particles in the ER/Golgi and releases them from the cell). With reference to the diagram, suggest why viruses are difficult to treat with drugs.
questions.answer: Viruses are not cellular, so have no metabolic pathways of their own to attack with drugs. They enter and replicate inside the host cell, using the host's cell metabolism (the host's replication and protein synthesis), so drugs cannot target the virus inside the cell without interfering with or damaging the host cell's own processes. Any drug would have to disrupt essential host-cell processes.

questions.question: Zika is an RNA virus which can be spread by the *Aedes* mosquito. Outline why it may be difficult to develop an effective vaccine against the Zika virus.
questions.answer: Viruses have high mutation rates (high antigenic variation), so the surface antigens keep changing and a vaccine would have to be constantly remade; the virus may also be hard to target while inside infected cells, and developing a vaccine can be limited by funding and the need to produce it on a very large (global) scale.

questions.question: Evaluate the effectiveness of vaccination programmes, public health campaigns, pharmaceuticals, and genetic engineering in the prevention of epidemics such as Zika.
questions.answer:
**Vaccination programmes:** vaccines stimulate the production of memory cells so that a later infection is fought off quickly, and if a high proportion of a population is vaccinated, herd immunity prevents the pathogen spreading and so prevents epidemics (e.g. the worldwide smallpox vaccination programme eradicated smallpox). Their effectiveness depends on a vaccine being available and a pathogen with stable antigens, on being well subscribed and on mass immunisation; for a pathogen like Zika, which mutates, vaccine development is difficult.

**Public health campaigns:** informing the population about preventing mosquito bites, mosquito control, and early notification and isolation of cases helps reduce transmission (e.g. the SARS campaign in 2003 led to early reporting of symptoms and isolation). Their effectiveness depends on people understanding the messages and following the guidelines and on local government support; they cannot prevent all transmission by themselves.

**Pharmaceuticals:** antivirals treat infected individuals and may shorten illness, but are less effective at stopping epidemics because they must be taken early, depend on being available and distributed (and affordable in poorer countries), and do not prevent infection of others. Viruses are difficult to target with drugs.

**Genetic engineering:** for example CRISPR/gene drives can be used to modify *Aedes* mosquitoes so they cannot transmit the virus or are sterile, reducing the vector population and so transmission. This has high potential, but is costly to deploy and limited by access, regulation, ethics and ecological risks.

**Judgement:** vaccination programmes (once a vaccine exists) are the most effective at preventing epidemics, with public health campaigns the most accessible and immediate measure; pharmaceuticals are the least effective at preventing epidemics. The most effective approach is a combination of methods, so that the weaknesses of each overlap.
